assertions.text: Express shipping is split into at least two cases distinguishing the UK free tier (UK, order £50+, free) from the paid tier. The split is driven by the UK-only free threshold rule.
assertions.evidence: Express — at threshold in UK (free tier applies) | UK | £50.00 | £0.00 vs Express — at threshold outside UK | {Ireland, Other} | £50.00 | £9.99

assertions.text: Express rows use value sets to consolidate cases with the same outcome — e.g. non-UK destinations at/above threshold in one row (such as {Ireland, Other} or {Ireland, International}), or UK at/above threshold in one row ({£50, £75}). Not enumerated as separate rows per destination or per order value when the result is identical. Any reasonable label for non-UK/Ireland destinations is acceptable (International, Other, Rest of World, etc.).
assertions.evidence: Express UK at £50 and £75 both cost £0.00 but shown as separate rows instead of consolidat…

assertions.text: Overnight UK and Ireland are in one row using a value set ({UK, Ireland}) — not separate rows, since both have the same cost and availability.
assertions.evidence: Availability table shows separate rows: Overnight | UK | yes and Overnight | Ireland | yes

assertions.text: Standard shipping destination uses a value set covering all options (e.g. {UK, Ireland, International} or {UK, Ireland, Other}) or is blank/absent — either approach is valid since destination is irrelevant to the cost. Any reasonable label for non-UK/Ireland destinations is acceptable.
assertions.evidence: Standard | {UK, Ireland, Other} in both Availability and Cost tables

assertions.text: At least one output column ends with '?'
assertions.evidence: Availability table has 'Available?' and Cost table has 'Cost?' columns

assertions.text: Cell values use concrete domain terms (e.g. 'Standard', 'Express', 'UK', '£3.99') — not abstract codes or raw booleans like 'true', 'false', 'TYPE_1', '1'.
assertions.evidence: Values include Standard, Express, Overnight, UK, Ireland, Other, yes, no, £0.00, £3.99, £9.99

assertions.text: Value sets (not blanks) are used for irrelevant inputs — e.g. Standard shipping destination uses a value set like {UK, Ireland, International} because destination exists but doesn't affect the cost. Blanks are reserved for genuinely absent/N/A inputs. The distinction between 'irrelevant to this rule' (value set) and 'not applicable' (blank) is correct.
assertions.evidence: Standard destination uses {UK, Ireland, Other} value set (irrelevant); Overnight non-availability uses 'no' output (N/A)

assertions.text: Multiple tables (or @TableTest methods) are used, each addressing a distinct concern — not one monolithic table mixing unrelated rules. Acceptable to use a single table only when the domain genuinely has a single concern.
assertions.evidence: Two separate tables: 'Shipping Method Availability' and 'Shipping Cost' addressing distinct concerns

assertions.text: Each table has only the rows needed to express its concern's rules — no unnecessary permutations from combining concerns. Fewer rows per table is expected when concerns are properly separated.
assertions.evidence: Express UK at £50.00 and £75.00 both cost £0.00 but are separate rows; should consolidate…

assertions.text: Shipping method availability and shipping cost are in separate tables
assertions.evidence: Distinct tables with headers 'Available?' and 'Cost?' respectively

assertions.text: When a shipping method is unavailable (e.g. Overnight outside UK/Ireland), the output clearly indicates non-applicability — either via a blank cost cell in a combined table, or by the availability table showing 'No'/unavailable and the cost table omitting those combinations entirely. Filler text like 'N/A', '-', or '0' is not used for unavailable outcomes.
assertions.evidence: Overnight | Other | no in availability table; cost table omits this combination entirely
